column2: Prologue
White Emperor City
The fate of the forsaken is to cross the wilderness, raise their battle banners once more, and return to their homeland.
Death is nothing to fear. It is only a long sleep.
Until I can devour this world, I would rather sleep in peace than wander alone.
We will wake again.
“Brother…” Someone was calling softly in the dark.
How annoying. Whose kid had gotten lost?
“Brother,” the child called again.
Annoying, annoying, annoying! Brother? No brothers here!
“Brother… I’m going now…” the child murmured, his voice fading into the distance.
Suddenly, he felt a little bad. There was a loneliness in that receding voice. He could almost see the child walking away, like an abandoned little hound.
“All right, all right, all right! What street do you live on? What number? Which door? What’s your useless brother’s name? I’ll take you home!” He rolled over and sat up.

He was sitting on the floor in the sunlight, dressed in white as luminous as the moon. Before him, a white camellia bloomed in a coarse porcelain vase. On the other side of the flower, the child, also in white, bent over a desk with an ink brush in his hand, carefully writing one stroke at a time.
Hey, you haven’t left? Were you messing with me? He wanted to say it, but didn’t.
Instead, he did something that felt perfectly natural. There was a plate of glistening green grapes on the table. He picked off a small cluster and passed it across to the child.
The child looked up, alarm flickering in his eyes like a startled young animal’s. “Brother, there are a lot of people outside.”
Bullshit. It’s so quiet, he thought.
But just as naturally, something else came out of his mouth. “We may die, I suppose. But don’t be afraid, Constantine.”
“I’m not afraid. As long as I’m with you, I’m not afraid… But why… won’t you eat me? If you ate me, there’s no prison you couldn’t break out of.” The child was completely serious.
Eat… you? Sure, you’re all pale and tender-looking, but that doesn’t mean you’d taste better than a hamburger. I had one for lunch. I’m not hungry at all, he thought.
“You would make fine food. But then I would be too lonely. For thousands of years, you’ve been the only one with me.” Once again, his words were nothing like his thoughts.

“But dying really is so sad. It’s like being sealed inside a black box, forever and ever, pitch-black… Like feeling your way through the night, but no matter how far you reach, your hands never touch a thing…”

“The fate of the forsaken is to cross the wilderness, raise their battle banners once more, and return to their homeland. Death is nothing to fear. It is only a long sleep. Until I can devour this world, I would rather sleep in peace than wander alone. We will wake again.” He could hardly believe such outrageously cool lines were coming out of his mouth.
“Brother… when you raise the battle banners and devour the world, will you eat me?” The child looked at him, something flickering in those clear eyes… anticipation.
What the hell? Was this a scene from We’re One Big Happy Cannibal Family? Your family values are seriously weird!
“Yes. And then you and I will reign over the world together!” Yet he nodded gently, his voice carrying a cold, unyielding authority.
The child poured a cup of water from a pitcher and handed it to him. He drank it in a daze.
“I’m leaving now, Brother. Goodbye.” The child stood up.
He wanted to say, I’m not your brother. You’ve got the wrong person. Instead, he merely said, “Goodbye. Take care of yourself. Humans… cannot be trusted.”
Another strange line, completely out of nowhere.
The child went outside and closed the door behind him. He listened as the footsteps grew fainter and fainter, until they disappeared altogether.

Suddenly, he was a little frightened. What had he been thinking, letting a child that small walk out into the streets alone? What if someone snatched him? Who knew how far he would have to go to find his brother? He grew restless. At last, unable to bear it any longer, he got up and ran for the door.

He pushed it open. Fierce light fell across his white clothes—not sunlight, but firelight. Beneath flames that scorched the sky, the city was screaming. Charred human figures ran through the fire. Thousands upon thousands of arrows rained down. A huge burning signboard tumbled from above, the words WHITE EMPEROR written across it. It was hell itself.
At the very center of the city stood a tall pole. The child hung at its top, his eyes closed, and all the flames in the city were burning him.
It was like some grand sacrifice.
His heart hurt so much, as though a knife were cutting into it. Someone precious had been lost, because he had made a mistake.
Then, suddenly, he remembered. Yes. He really was that child’s brother.
“Constan… tine.” He called the name.
He jerked upright, opening his eyes in the afternoon sunlight, gasping for breath and drenched in cold sweat. Outside came the rumble of a train passing on the elevated tracks.
All at once, that noise sounded wonderful. It reminded him that everything in the dream had been false. He was here, in the ordinary human world.
Act One
The Gate to Cassell

A few times in every life, you feel as though you have seen the gates of heaven swing open. Lu Mingfei had waited eighteen years. At the lowest, most pathetic moment of his life, the gates finally opened.
The angel who walked in swept her gaze around the room, her eyes sharp as knives.
Lu Mingfei typed “GG”—“Good Game,” a compliment to your opponent in competitive gaming, and also an admission of defeat—and exited the game.
The last image on the screen was of twelve Terran battlecruisers concentrating their Yamato cannon fire on his Hatchery, turning it into a pool of blood.

He had lost his sixth match of the day. Zero wins, six losses. He had held out for twenty-two minutes and twenty-three seconds in the last one, but had gone down in the end. His opponent had excellent micro, and he played Terran. Marines were an absurdly overpowered unit in StarCraft: no delay before firing, just raise the gun and shoot, lower it and run. Lu Mingfei’s Zerglings couldn’t catch them, and got picked off one after another along the way.

His opponent was crowing in the chat. “You don’t necessarily need tanks when you play Terran against Zerg. The Korean pros don’t even build tanks. You just pump out units right from the start, send in a ton of Marines mixed with Medics, keep wearing them down while you push…”
Lu Mingfei could picture the guy’s smug, animated face.

He said nothing and switched to QQ. The avatar of the girl in a baseball cap was still gray and motionless. She hadn’t come online. Another pointless wait. He scratched his head, a little disappointed. A different avatar began bouncing instead: a panda with an eminently punchable face. The screen name was “Old Tang.”
“You’re pretty good with Zerg, bro. Let’s go again sometime!” Old Tang was the guy who had beaten him. “It’s just your micro that needs work. Your strategy’s solid.”
“Sure,” Lu Mingfei said.
Old Tang logged off, full of himself. Lu Mingfei stuck his tongue out at the screen.

If Old Tang had seen how Lu Mingfei was actually playing, he probably wouldn’t have felt so pleased. He would have called him a freak and never played him again. Lu Mingfei was using an old IBM laptop with no mouse attached, controlling everything with the little red pointing stick. Only a lunatic would play StarCraft on a pointing stick. It was like cleaning your ears with a rolling pin. If he plugged in a mouse, Old Tang probably wouldn’t make it to the eight-minute mark. But then how would he kill the time?
Besides, Lu Mingfei couldn’t be bothered to explain that he was only making things harder for himself out of boredom. He had a lot of time to kill. What if Old Tang refused to play next time?
But however much time he killed, she still didn’t come online.
Why bother? Sometimes he asked himself that. Waiting and waiting like an idiot, four hours for two or three lines of conversation. It hardly seemed worth it.
But who could calculate what something like that was worth?

“A case of that milk in bags that’s on sale, half a jin of Cantonese sausage, and the new issue of Fiction Illustrated for Mingze. Come straight back when you’re done, and trim the celery on the table! And check the gatehouse for letters from America! Still playing games? You don’t care about your own future at all! If nobody admits you, do you think you can get into a first-tier university on your exam scores? All that money we’ve spent on you—what good has it done?” His aunt’s voice thundered from the next room.

His head buzzing, Lu Mingfei rattled off a string of yeses and scurried out. The hallway was quiet. Afternoon sunlight came through the window at the end of the stairwell, spilling warm across him. Pure white sheets hung along the corridor. Outside, the wind stirred glossy green leaves with a rustling sound. He leaned against the door, listening to his aunt’s endless complaints inside. With the door between them, it seemed to belong to another world.
Spring again. Lu Mingfei, senior in high school, nearly eighteen.

He lived with his uncle and aunt and had a younger cousin named Lu Mingze. He attended the most prestigious private high school in the city: steep tuition, stern teachers, luxury cars streaming past, beautiful girls drifting by like clouds. In three months and four days, he would have to sit the national college entrance exam. These days, everyone he met earnestly informed him that doomsday was approaching and he ought to get fired up.
But the more pressure there was, the lazier Lu Mingfei became. When he wasn’t playing StarCraft, he lay on his bed staring at the ceiling.
For someone whose presence barely registered, his laziness was easy enough to understand.

Lu Mingfei hadn’t seen his parents in more than six years. The good news was that they were supposedly still alive, and wrote him a letter every six months. The bad news was that every time they wrote, his mother regretfully explained that their plan to return to China to visit him had been postponed again, because “there have been new developments.”

His parents were both archaeologists, supposedly working on a major project whose results, once announced, would astonish the world as much as Sven Hedin’s discovery of ancient Loulan. In middle school, Lu Mingfei had been very proud of them. He read lots of books about archaeology and talked about it enthusiastically with his classmates on the way home. But he soon realized that the ones who should be proud were the guys whose parents came to pick them up. After school, a pack of boys would saunter down the street side by side, taking up nearly half the road. Then a car horn would sound behind them, and one of the guys would instantly stop swaggering, climb obediently into the family car, and disappear. One by one they peeled away, until usually only Lu Mingfei remained, still swaggering along by himself.

Looking out through their car windows, the others watched him kick a stone and wander freely into the distance, and envied him terribly. He could go anywhere he wanted. Browse a mall, buy a snack, even shoot some pool.
“Lu Mingfei’s family treats him the best. They never make him do anything.”

In fact, when Lu Mingfei was alone, he didn’t browse malls or play pool. Once he had sat in the internet café long enough to feel sick of it, he went home. But after entering the building, he didn’t go inside the apartment. He squeezed through the iron grating that led to the roof, sat beside a humming air-conditioning unit, and looked out over the city until the sun went down.

Lu Mingfei thought of his parents as Superman and Superwoman. Perhaps if the plane they were on crashed one day, they would finally appear before him, holding it up as they brought it safely to earth. Otherwise, they would always be busy saving the world, rather than doing anything for him, Lu Mingfei. Superhero parents were certainly something to brag about. In practice, though, they might as well not exist. He could barely remember what they looked like anymore. Only when he occasionally looked at an old family photograph could he faintly recall that man and woman, and their old house with its walls covered in Virginia creeper.

What interested his uncle and aunt more was the money his parents regularly sent from abroad. Thanks to that money, Lu Mingfei could attend an elite private high school. Thanks to it, his uncle and aunt could buy a small-engine BMW, his uncle could afford convincing counterfeit designer goods, and his aunt had money to lose at mahjong. Thanks to it, his cousin Lu Mingze had acquired the nickname “Crown Prince Ze” at school. The cousins attended the same high school. Lu Mingze not only had better grades, but dressed more carefully, and whenever girls joined him for a meal, he insisted on paying. His parents even dressed especially well for his parent-teacher conferences, leaving everyone with the impression that he was a child raised in a jar of honey.
If Lu Mingze hadn’t been 160 centimeters tall and weighed 160 jin—eighty kilos—he probably would have found a girlfriend long ago.
And Lu Mingfei was merely “Lu Mingze’s older cousin.”
Lu Mingfei didn’t particularly mind. Even his parents didn’t care about him. How much could he ask of an uncle and aunt?

With both hands in his pockets, his head drooping and his eyes on the ground, Lu Mingfei went downstairs. He bought what his aunt wanted at the convenience store, then wandered over to the bookstall for the latest Fiction Illustrated.

His aunt thought Lu Mingze was clever, studious, ambitious, and especially devoted to literature. Even reading Fiction Illustrated became “our Mingze is studying” in her mouth. Every time a new issue appeared, she took it as another development in Chinese youth literature and hurried Lu Mingfei out to buy it so Mingze could keep up.

The old man at the newsstand downstairs thought Lu Mingfei was both melancholy and a bit of a freeloader, with a passion for literature. He was always buying Fiction Illustrated, though he never read it. Instead, he squatted beside the stand and read the latest Home Computers and Games for free, tossed it back, frankly declared that it was getting worse and worse, dusted off his pants, and left.

Lu Mingfei had a quietly sneaky streak. Lu Mingze was forever saying things like “in my house” and ordering his cousin to do this or that. Lu Mingfei always complied. Then, out of sheer pettiness, he visited Lu Mingze’s secret Qzone page.

After reading some literature, Lu Mingze had adopted the pen name “Lonely Snake” and copied a great many sorrowful sentences onto his Qzone, alongside close-up selfies taken on his phone. Occasionally he uploaded pictures of his wrists smeared with red ink to look as if he had cut them, with poems more or less saying that without love he might as well die. Lu Mingfei knew his cousin’s romantic instincts were stirring. At school, any budding romance died the moment the girl saw him in daylight, so now he was hoping for a thunderous collision of souls on QQ.

Lu Mingfei registered a new QQ account under the name “Sunset’s Imprint.” He uploaded a photo of a cute, short-haired girl, entered his age as sixteen, and set his status to “Let your smiles and sorrows leave their imprint on my life.” While Lu Mingze was online at home, he slipped off to an internet café and struck up a conversation with Lonely Snake. Before long, Lu Mingze apparently felt that his little snake had finally found something delicious, and was more than happy to let his smiles and sorrows leave their imprint on a girl’s life. At home, he cheerfully hummed Shin’s “Parting Song” every day; on QQ, he kept asking to meet, ready to launch into an earth-shattering romance. Lu Mingfei agreed with absolute conviction, but always set the date for when his aunt would be dragging Lu Mingze off to piano lessons. Each time, the lovely girl slipped through his cousin’s fingers, leaving him bitterly distraught and lending his renditions of “Parting Song” a rather mournful note.
It was the happiest thing that had happened to Lu Mingfei lately.
That was the sort of person Lu Mingfei was. Not especially good, not particularly capable of doing anything bad. Almost eighteen, and he still had no idea where his future lay.
“Mingfei, I hear you’re going abroad to study,” the old newsstand owner said idly.
“Hardly. I’ve only applied. Who’d take me?” Lu Mingfei was squatting beside the stand, helping himself to a magazine.
“Studying abroad is good. Come back with a foreign degree, and you’ll make plenty of money.”
“I don’t want plenty of money. If I can’t get into college, I’ll help you run the stand. Just pay me enough to buy PS2 games.”
“No ambition. There’s no money in running a newsstand. I only do it because I’m old.”
Lu Mingfei rolled his eyes up toward the sunlight filtering through the green leaves. “Seems pretty nice. You can sit in the sun, space out when no one’s around, and watch pretty girls go by.”

The subject rather depressed him. He had applied to American universities, but certainly not because his grades were so dazzling that he stood much chance. Everyone had a different way of assessing his academic performance. His homeroom teacher said, “Lu Mingfei, were you born a lead weight? Do you have any idea how much you single-handedly drag down our class average?” His aunt told his uncle, “Mingze gets his good grades from my side of the family. Just look at your family’s genes. Hopeless!” Only Lu Mingze showed him any consideration, encouraging him on QQ: “Sunset! So what if your grades are bad? People like us have to walk our own path! As far as I’m concerned, you’re a wonderful girl!”

The idea of sending him abroad had come to his aunt in a flash of inspiration, and she had championed it single-handedly. She stood over him while he filled in the applications and generously paid the several-dozen-dollar fee for each school. She had her reasons. English was the only subject Lu Mingfei was decent at. When he tagged along with his English-obsessed classmates to take the TOEFL, he had enjoyed a spectacular stroke of dumb luck and scored well. With his grades, a first-tier Chinese university was a long shot. Skipping the national exam to study abroad was fashionable these days. They could try the applications, and if another stroke of dumb luck landed him an American acceptance letter, she would have something to show for all the money his parents had sent.

His aunt also had a second, “smaller” calculation. Lu Mingze’s grades were a little better than Lu Mingfei’s, but hardly outstanding. He couldn’t get into the famous universities she was always talking about, like Tsinghua or Peking University. Skipping the exam to study abroad would be a respectable alternative. But college determined your whole life; she couldn’t bear to let Mingze take that risk. After much thought, she seemed to recall some famous saying about how “every difficult path must first be trodden by the tough soles of the brave.” Suddenly, Lu Mingfei struck her as very brave indeed. She would have him use those tough soles to tread a path for Lu Mingze. If he failed, no harm done. It would merely prove the path was blocked. Lu Mingfei could wait a year and take the entrance exam alongside his cousin.
Unfortunately, courage alone clearly couldn’t open that difficult path. It was strewn with ankle-twisting stones. More than a dozen replies had already arrived, and their openings were much alike:
“Dear Applicant:
Thank you for your interest in our college. We regret to inform you…”

Several hundred dollars in application fees had bought his aunt nothing but repeated expressions of gratitude from Americans. Charity was proving painful. Lu Mingfei, meanwhile, was neither anxious nor impatient. He had the serene stillness of an old monk in meditation. He merely squeezed out a sorrowful expression whenever another rejection arrived, to keep his aunt company in her disappointment.
Only one university had yet to reply: the most highly ranked of the prestigious schools, the University of Chicago.
“Any mail for me?” Lu Mingfei poked his head around the gatehouse door, putting on an English accent. “Mingfei Lu.”
“Yes. From America.” The guard tossed out a letter.

Lu Mingfei felt the envelope. One thin sheet of paper. Definitely a rejection. Acceptance letters came with forms and informational materials, a whole thick stack. Thanking you for your application and regretting that you hadn’t been admitted took only a single printed page.
He tore the envelope open. To his surprise, the letter was written in Chinese:
Dear Mr. Lu Mingfei:
Thank you for your interest in the University of Chicago. We regret to inform you that you have not been admitted.
However, as we often say, there is more than one road. The question is whether you are willing to take it.

Allow us first to introduce ourselves. Cassell College is a private institution located on the far outskirts of Chicago, Illinois, in the United States. We are affiliated with the University of Chicago and maintain extensive academic exchanges with it.

We have had the honor of receiving your application materials from the University of Chicago. Following a careful evaluation, we believe you meet Cassell College’s admission requirements and would like to extend this invitation to you.
Please contact our Professor Guderian as soon as you receive this letter. He is currently on an academic visit to China and will arrange your interview.

Should you have any questions, please also contact Professor Guderian. I will assist him in providing any help you may require. My name is Norma Lawrence, secretary of Cassell College. It is a great pleasure to make your acquaintance.
Yours sincerely,
Norma
Lu Mingfei lowered the letter and felt his forehead, rather dazed.

It had begun perfectly normally, a standard rejection letter. How had everything changed after “However, as we often say, there is more than one road. The question is whether you are willing to take it”? Apparently, he was already on an interview list. Some of his high school classmates had successfully applied abroad, but an American professor traveling all this way to interview someone was a first. Lu Mingfei couldn’t imagine what he had done to deserve it. He hadn’t even contributed an application fee to this Cassell College.
Had Lu Mingze discovered Sunset’s Imprint’s true identity? Was this some elaborate revenge?
But the postmark on the envelope really was from Illinois, USA.

He tipped the envelope upside down. Apart from that one sheet of expensive paper, there was nothing else inside. That settled it: this had to be a scam. It told him to contact some Professor Guderian immediately, but didn’t even give him a phone number. The thought actually made him feel a little better.
“Sign here.” The guard tossed him another slip.
“You have to sign for letters?” Lu Mingfei asked, puzzled.
“A package came with it. You have to sign for that.”
Still confused, Lu Mingfei signed and received a large FedEx envelope with something hard inside. He hesitated, tore it open, and tipped out… a phone.
An all-black N96.
Lu Mingfei felt he needed a moment to collect himself. He switched it on. The battery was actually more than half full. There was a single entry in the contacts: Professor Guderian.
“Definitely a con artist! And someone who lives in this complex! Only someone who knows us would know our situation!” His aunt slapped the letter and delivered her verdict with absolute certainty.

“But what con artist would spend that much? It’s an N96! Even a gray-market one costs over four thousand yuan. An official one’s over five thousand!” His uncle kept covering the black phone with fingerprints, like an old woman caressing a jade bangle passed down through the family.

His uncle was a man of taste. Lu Mingfei had once had the privilege of accompanying him to dinner and watching him set his phone down with his left hand and his lighter with his right, each landing on the table with just the right weight. In the course of conversation, he casually rolled up his sleeve to reveal a high-quality fake Montblanc watch bought in Guangzhou, winning unanimous praise for his taste. Lately, he had mentioned more than once to Lu Mingze that the new N96 was very “high-end” and suited him perfectly. But his aunt, who controlled the family finances, had given him a firm “No!”

“What Cassell College? It’s got to be after our money! Affiliated with the University of Chicago, my foot. Chu Zihang, who ranked first in our school, went abroad last year to a college affiliated with Chicago, too. One of his cousins is a university professor and already has a green card. Those colleges affiliated with famous universities are practically Ivy League. Even Americans can’t get in!” Lu Mingze rarely took such an interest in his older cousin’s future.

Lu Mingfei knew Chu Zihang was Lu Mingze’s idol. When most of the other students were still wearing Nike and Adidas, Chu Zihang was already into brands like Burberry. He would loosely knot a Burberry scarf over a Diesel pullover and walk down the corridor with an expressionless face, and the whole school would call his look British. Once, two girls had been disciplined for clawing each other’s faces over “whose Chu Zihang was,” even though he had never so much as spoken to either of them.
Lu Mingze recounted this senior’s exploits to Sunset’s Imprint, declaring inspirationally that one day he would proudly prove to the whole school that he was every bit as good as Chu Zihang.

Lu Mingfei thought the real issue was all those flirtatious looks from girls across the grade. Lu Mingze cared more about “how to become a male lion ruling over a pride of lionesses” than about being as accomplished as Chu Zihang.

Lu Mingfei didn’t envy Chu Zihang at all. Sometimes he thought, These people treat Chu Zihang like an idol, but none of them knows what he’s doing in America. Maybe he’s washing dishes in a restaurant. Without anyone teaching him, he had developed something of Ah Q’s knack for consoling himself.
His Chinese teacher once held up his essay as a bad example and savaged it in class, saying it showed no imagination, only pessimism—just like its author, who had no ambition whatsoever.
Lu Mingfei had felt a little like standing up and saying that he had fantasies, too.

Once, after watching all three Matrix films back-to-back, he had suddenly felt that he must possess some extraordinary ability that had yet to be discovered. Like Neo, he was “the One.” One day, a mysterious figure would come to uncover his power. Beneath everyone’s blazing gaze, he would transform… and do something that shook the world.

But while delivering his criticism, the Chinese teacher had his lofty gaze fixed on the dozing students in the back rows and didn’t spare Lu Mingfei so much as a sidelong glance. Lu Mingfei could only duck his head and abandon his explanation of his inner journey.

No one would discuss this magnificent idea with him, so he kept elaborating the details by himself. By senior year, the fantasy had acquired a full set of scenes. Whenever the school held its Lunar New Year gala, the pretty little piano prodigy Liu Miaomiao, who had passed the Grade Ten exam, would play onstage while the boys in her class danced around the piano in matching black formalwear. Lu Mingfei would sit in a forgotten corner with his chin in his hand, imagining that perhaps a helicopter would descend from the sky to collect him. Men in black suits and dark glasses would enter the hall with the icy efficiency of CIA agents in a movie and say in low voices, “Mr. Lu Mingfei, this is no time for a New Year’s show. The organization needs you.” They would put him in a black military uniform and a long trench coat, then escort him out under the eyes of his classmates. Outside, a black helicopter would roar, its great rotors whipping up a wind that cut across their faces like knives. Then the pretty Liu Miaomiao and all the dancing boys would stop and stare blankly at his retreating back.
The point of the story was never how he would save the world. It was the way everyone else would look at him as he left.
So. Damn. Cool.

Lu Mingfei knew perfectly well that the fantasy was only a way to pass the time. But he could find nothing about himself to be proud of. As far as he could tell, his future would be to attend some obscure college, fall in love there, then graduate, find a job, and rent an apartment. Perhaps when his parents occasionally remembered him, they would urge him to get married. So he would marry, have a child, and go to work every day.

And now, with this letter from America, something was actually going to disturb the stagnant pool of his life. Yet in the family meeting, he felt like an outsider, huddled in one corner of the sofa with his hands placed obediently on his knees, while the endless chatter of his uncle, aunt, and Lu Mingze filled the living room.

He stood and left. No one noticed the departure of the person at the center of it all. The other three kept arguing about whether the interview invitation was real. His aunt and Lu Mingze seemed rather shaken. If it was genuine, it was a spectacular stroke of dumb luck, the kind that didn’t come to anyone once in ten years, and somehow it had come to Lu Mingfei. His aunt wasn’t used to seeing this droopy boy suddenly perk up. How was Mingze supposed to outdo him now?

Lu Mingfei returned to his room, logged onto QQ, and stared at the baseball-cap girl’s avatar. Still gray. Offline or invisible—either way, no message. He glanced at the clock on the wall. It had been eighteen hours since he had left Chen Wenwen a message asking whether she would attend the literary club activity tomorrow night.

Chen Wenwen didn’t actually wear baseball caps. Her long hair was soft, fine, straight, and lovely; it needed no covering. Lu Mingfei had met her on the first day of school. She had arrived discreetly in a Passat, wearing a white cotton dress and white ankle socks edged with lace, a Hello Kitty clip in her long hair. The most dazzling girl in his class should have been Su Xiaoqiang, the “Little Celestial Princess.” That day she had arrived in a Mercedes S500, dressed head to toe in DKNY, pride dancing in every glance. After waving goodbye to her coal-business father, she had gone to register, appraising the boys in her new class and expecting their admiring looks in return. But the boys were all stealing glances toward a corner by the window. Having finished her paperwork, Chen Wenwen sat there on a bench with a copy of Marguerite Duras’s The Lover. Sunlight shone on her cotton dress and skin, making everything seem translucent.

After fifteen years of being the proudest girl around, the Little Celestial Princess had lost to a young literary type on her very first day of high school. She seethed. To make things worse, a tactless boy beside her pointed toward Chen Wenwen and said quietly, “I guess she’s the prettiest girl in our new class.”
When had the Little Celestial Princess ever suffered such humiliation? She stamped hard on his foot and turned away.
That boy was Lu Mingfei.

Really, Lu Mingfei was an honest person. He thought Chen Wenwen was prettier than the Little Celestial Princess, so he said so. How could he have known it would earn him a three-year feud? There had been seven or eight boys admiring Chen Wenwen, all thinking the same thing. The others simply understood the principle of “admiring in silence.” Later, those boys formed a literary club with Chen Wenwen at its center. They met every week to read cold, sorrowful works of European and American literature and wrote reading responses for the Chinese teacher to mark. Lu Mingfei’s uncle described these as books for “middle-class white women” and couldn’t understand how someone as scatterbrained as Lu Mingfei had become a club officer.

To Lu Mingfei, Chen Wenwen was the first girl he had ever idolized, his model of the good girl who would make a happy home. At fifteen, he had thought there could be no greater happiness in the world than marrying her. He believed he had a tiny chance because she had personally invited him to join the club. As president, Chen Wenwen had invited only two members: Lu Mingfei and Zhao Menghua, whom the Little Celestial Princess was determined to have for herself. Zhao Menghua was easy to describe. Of everyone in the school, he was the likeliest to become “the next Chu Zihang.”
Zhao Menghua was applying abroad, too, and hadn’t received any offers either. Yet this muddleheaded Cassell College had sent an interview invitation to Lu Mingfei.

“Up for a match?” A big-faced cat avatar was flashing on QQ. The name was “Nono.” Lu Mingfei couldn’t remember adding this person, but he never turned down an invitation. Few enough people added him in the first place.
“Sure,” he replied absently.

Lu Mingfei was still using the pointing stick. Something was on his mind, he felt sluggish, and Nono sounded like a girl’s name. The genuinely good players in the channel were all middle-aged-guy types. But he soon discovered that this opponent was not only vicious but cunning. The moment his attention wandered, two Zerglings ambushed the Drone he had sent to scout. Losing one Drone was no big deal, but that neat little trap put him on his guard. He reinforced his base and sent six Zerglings to patrol nearby. It saved him. He spotted the enemy squad of Zerglings the instant they entered his territory. Their chance at a surprise attack gone, they had to pull back at once.
Lu Mingfei didn’t dare get careless again. He plugged in the mouse.

Only then did the real battle begin. Both sides upgraded their main forces from Zerglings to Hydralisks, and both simultaneously sent Mutalisks on air raids while their Hydralisks attacked, opening up a second front. By the time the Queens appeared, the fighting was white-hot. Each player had four bases. Mixed armies fought a savage tug-of-war over the open ground in the center, splashing sheets of blood across the battlefield. Sweat broke out on Lu Mingfei’s forehead. His hands danced over the keyboard as if he were playing the piano. It couldn’t be easy for the other player, either. The way they were pushing their micro was close to professional level. He had never faced anyone this strong. His competitive streak stirred, and he decided to risk upgrading his main base to tier three and bringing out the “three-horse team”: Devourers, Guardians, and Ultralisks. It was a fundamental shift in strategy. If his opponent hesitated even briefly and failed to attack while he was spending his resources on the upgrade, victory would be his.

The progress bar crept forward. His heart raced and his palms sweated. To bluff, he added a squad of Hydralisks and three Lurkers outside. If his opponent believed he was massing a large army and held back, she would have fallen for it. Those were all the troops he had. Every other resource had gone into the upgrade.
Almost there. Once the upgrade finished and the three-horse team appeared, he could advance through the air and on the ground, steadily picking off enemy bases one after another.
Lu Mingfei could see the first light of victory.
“You’re teching to tier three.” A line of text appeared at the bottom of the screen.
Lu Mingfei froze.
“Just quit. I’ve got four squads of Hydras and four of Lings, all with level-two attack and armor,” Nono continued typing.

The progress bar was almost full, but Lu Mingfei could only type “GG.” As she typed, Nono had shared her vision with him. Outside his main base, still upgrading to tier three, her army was massed. Once it attacked, the victory would be crushing.
Lu Mingfei left the game, returned to QQ, and told Nono, “Respect!”
Nono didn’t answer. She left a grinning, big-toothed laughing emoji and logged off.

For the first time in his life, Lu Mingfei felt that someone had seen right through him. It was like a dearest friend, gone for years, coming back to find him. He sat there in a daze for a while, then clicked on Nono’s profile. It was blank. He searched his memory and was certain he had never known a StarCraft player that good—much less a girl.
Chen Wenwen’s avatar was bouncing in his contact list, but it was gray. She had come online and already left.
“Sure. See you the day after tomorrow.” That was her message.

He had waited almost nineteen hours for those few words. But his low spirits seemed to evaporate. He jumped onto his bed, whistled, wiggled his hips, and beamed, completely forgetting that Nono had beaten him.

When Lu Mingze entered their shared bedroom, he looked his older cousin up and down and said impatiently, “Mom and Dad called that Professor Guderian. Your interview’s at the Regent Hotel the day after tomorrow. They said you should get ready.”
